newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - CLT/Bertelsmann UFA merger ok'd - EU source.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - CLT/Bertelsmann UFA merger ok'd - EU source.

text.p: The European Commission cleared on Monday the merger between Luxembourg-based broadcaster CLT, which is controllled by Audiofina, and Bertelsmann's television unit UFA, an EU source said.

The operation will create Europe's largest television alliance in terms of revenue. It will focus mainly on free-acces TV after the two partners in September dropped plans to launch a digital pay-television channel in Germany.

After a routine one-month probe, the Commission concluded that the operation would not lead to the creation of a dominant position, not even in Germany where the two partners are both active, the source said.
This was because they would face competition from commercial television channels linked to rival group operated by Bavarian media mogul Leo Kirch, the source added.
An official statement is expected later on Monday or possibly Tuesday.

The clearance of the alliance between the two strong media players comes as little surprise after European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said that the abandonment of the pay-television plans made the Commission's approval easier.
But it comes as a relief for the sector, which has had to put up with a particularly tough Commission regarding media ventures in the past years.
Under the terms of the agreement, CLT and UFA will be merged in a joint venture which will be jointly controlled by Bertelsmann and Audiofina.
CLT and UFA are already partners in a number of German TV operations including the country's largest commercial channel RTL.
An alliance in the pay-television area could have eroded the position of Premiere, a pay-per-view channel owned by Bertelsmann, Canal Plus and Kirch.
The Commission blocked in 1994 a proposed joint venture between Bertelsmann, Kirch and Deutsche Telekom to provide services for pay-TV due to fears it would close the market for newcomers.

Last year, it also also banned two media joint ventures in the Netherlands and in the Nordic market, bringing to three the number of media deals blocked out of a total of only five negative rulings since 1990 -- when the Commission became the EU's clearing house for large mergers and acquisitions.
